title: Operation Neretva '93: The ARBiH Strikes Back in Herzegovina
sources: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II, pp. 434-435, September 1993 fighting east of Prozor and along the Neretva
ICTY Halilovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-48-T, 16 November 2005), Operation Neretva command record and Grabovica/Uzdol findings
source_note: Balkan Battlegrounds supplies the bounded September 1993 operational chronology: the 14 September offensive east of Prozor, movement south from Jablanica and Dreznica, fighting at Vrdi, and the 17 September East Mostar attack. The Halilovic Trial Judgment supplies the operation's command and crime-case context but does not support attributing superior responsibility after the acquittal. Unsupported strategic objectives, campaign rankings, and diplomatic causation are omitted; no source prose is copied.
content:
Operation Neretva '93 belongs to the September 1993 fighting between the ARBiH and HVO in northern Herzegovina. Balkan Battlegrounds records a sizable ARBiH offensive east of Prozor on 14 September 1993 after months of inconclusive fighting around Konjic and Jablanica. The chronology supports a bounded account of several connected attacks, not a claim that one operation produced a decisive strategic result.

Between Prozor and Jablanica, the ARBiH 44th Neretva Brigade moved the confrontation line west. Government forces also advanced south from Jablanica and Dreznica toward Mostar and took a band of territory along the highway. Around Vrdi, an ARBiH infantry attack on 19 September failed after artillery preparation; a later attack began on 4 October and entered the town the next day, but Vrdi remained on the confrontation line.

Further south, ARBiH forces attacked from East Mostar on 17 September and made limited gains before HVO forces blocked aid convoys and intensified artillery fire. Fighting continued until another Mostar ceasefire took effect on 3 October. The local record therefore shows advances and continued combat without a decisive breakthrough in the Neretva corridor.

The ICTY Halilovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-48-T) examined the operation through the prosecution of Sefer Halilovic and the crimes committed at Grabovica and Uzdol. The judgment found that ARBiH personnel committed crimes at those villages but acquitted Halilovic because his superior authority and effective control over the perpetrators were not proved beyond reasonable doubt. Operational coordination and individual criminal liability are separate questions in that record.

This essay therefore confines the operation to the places, dates, movements, and limited outcomes supported by Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II, pp. 434-435, while the paired Grabovica/Uzdol record carries the tribunal's crime findings and command-liability outcome.
